title: Trump, Xi, and Putin Meet in Shenzhen as Anthropic's $1.5T IPO Fails to Halt a $4 Trillion AI Rout, and Bahrain and Poland Face Escalating Strikes
subhead: During the week of November 16–22, US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin held a landmark trilateral summit in Shenzhen without Europe or Ukraine; Anthropic's record $1.5 trillion IPO was overtaken by an SEC accounting probe into Nvidia and a $4 trillion Wall Street AI wipeout that erased Nasdaq's 2026 gains; and Russian missiles landed in Poland while Iranian drones and missiles struck Bahrain.

sections.heading: Shenzhen Summit Excludes Kyiv and Europe as Russian Missiles Land in Poland
sections.body:
SCMP, BBC, NPR, and Al Jazeera — Great-power diplomacy dominated the week of November 16–22 as US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin convened for an unprecedented trilateral summit in Shenzhen during APEC, leaving Ukraine and its European allies outside the room (NPR, SCMP). While US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Trump and Xi agreed that humans must remain in the loop on military AI decisions (Defense News, SCMP), concrete disarmament or ceasefire breakthroughs remained elusive. By Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called Putin a 'killer' after Trump referred to the Russian leader as a 'friend' (BBC, CNA).

On the ground, fighting sharpened rather than cooled: Russian air strikes damaged the Austrian and Dutch embassies in Kyiv (Euronews), Ukraine defended strikes on the Crimean Bridge as a fair response to 109 Russian attacks on Ukrainian bridges (BBC), and on Friday two Russian missiles and a suspected drone landed in southeastern Poland during nearby European allied exercises, prompting Prime Minister Donald Tusk to denounce a Moscow provocation (BBC, SCMP). Meanwhile, Denmark expelled a Russian diplomat over an alleged plot to kill a Ukrainian rapper, and Britain and the EU inked a post-Brexit reset deal in Brussels even as talks over university tuition fees continued (Al Jazeera, TRT World, The Guardian).
sections.whyItMatters: The Shenzhen summit underscored a return to three-power bargaining over European security heads, while Russian projectiles hitting Poland showed how thin the buffer around NATO drills remains.

sections.heading: Nvidia's SEC Probe and a $4 Trillion AI Wipeout Overshadow Anthropic's $1.5T IPO
sections.body:
New York Times, Wall Street Journal, CNBC, and Bloomberg — Technology and equity markets endured their sharpest reversal since 2023 despite Anthropic completing a record-breaking IPO at a $1.5 trillion valuation after selling 1.127 billion shares (CNBC, Anadolu Agency). Investor enthusiasm quickly soured after reports revealed the US Securities and Exchange Commission opened an accounting investigation into Nvidia amid questions over Asian chip sales and former CEO Jensen Huang's resignation, alongside congressional disclosures that Washington had approved nearly 880,000 advanced AI chips for Chinese firms earlier this year (New York Times, SCMP).

Nvidia shares plunged 14% on Friday to sit 48% below their peak—completing their worst weekly streak since 2008—while the Nasdaq Composite erased its 2026 gains and combined AI equity losses reached $4 trillion on Wall Street and $1.7 trillion in China, spilling into a drop in Bitcoin below $60,000 before a partial rebound (CNBC, WSJ, Bloomberg). Over the weekend, Huang signaled willingness to return as Nvidia CEO as Trump urged giving him a 'second chance' (WSJ, Al Jazeera). Separately, US digital security faced acute strain as a classified US intelligence network went down and the FBI investigated an apparent hack of its National Crime Information Center database (WSJ, BBC, NBC News).
sections.whyItMatters: Anthropic's mega-IPO could not rescue AI valuations once accounting scrutiny at Nvidia and export-control leaks exposed governance fragility at the core of the AI hardware boom.

sections.heading: Iran War Widens to Bahrain and Hormuz Mines as Turkey Defines Mecca Pact Limits
sections.body:
Times of Israel, Anadolu Agency, The War Zone, and OilPrice — Military pressure across the Middle East persisted even as Washington weighed diplomatic openings. Early in the week, US lawmakers rejected a Senate war-powers curb on Iran (48–51) as Pentagon officials put the war's cost at $48.3 billion, while US forces expanded their naval blockade of Iranian ports to ship-to-ship cargo transfers and the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group arrived to relieve the USS George Washington (Anadolu Agency, USNI News, The War Zone).

Over the weekend, Iran targeted US Patriot radar positions in Bahrain and damaged an industrial facility in the kingdom, Houthis launched ballistic missiles toward Riyadh and triggered an early warning alert in Mecca, and UKMTO reported oil tanker strikes near Oman in the Strait of Hormuz (Times of Israel, Anadolu Agency, CNBC). Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan clarified that Ankara's Mecca Defense Alliance commitments focus on defending Saudi Arabia with no decision to deploy troops to Yemen, while noting Washington lifted ammunition purchase holds even as CAATSA hurdles remain (Anadolu Agency, TRT World). In oil markets, Brent dropped 5% toward $91–$92 on looming surplus forecasts despite tanker attacks, while Saudi Arabia expanded crude storage in Japan (OilPrice).
sections.whyItMatters: Iranian strikes hitting Bahrain and tanker attacks off Oman demonstrate Tehran's ability to impose regional costs even as global crude markets price oversupply over conflict risk.

sections.heading: Washington Restricts Canada Defense Ties as Europe and Turkey Push Autonomous Systems
sections.body:
Washington Post, Breaking Defense, Defense News, and Anadolu Agency — Transatlantic defense politics shifted sharply after Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth issued a classified memo restricting military cooperation and socialization with Canada, prompting Ottawa to join NATO's innovation fund while insisting bilateral operations remain business as usual (Washington Post, The Hill, Defense One). At the same time, the Pentagon inspector general launched an audit into defense start-up contracts, the US Air Force awarded a $16 billion propulsion contract to 58 firms, and the CBO warned the US Navy's shipbuilding plan exceeds budget estimates by $234 billion (Washington Post, Breaking Defense, USNI News).

Across Europe and Turkey, indigenous capabilities accelerated: Baykar delivered the first three operational Bayraktar KIZILELMA uncrewed fighter jets to Turkish forces alongside new indigenous missile and drone deliveries (Anadolu Agency, TRT World); Germany cleared live-fire trials for attack drones as Auterion partnered with Ukraine's Skyfall to build drones in Germany; and NATO launched its commercial satellite launch initiative (Defense News, Breaking Defense).
sections.whyItMatters: Pentagon friction with Canada and $234 billion US shipbuilding shortfalls contrast with rapid European and Turkish fielding of operational combat drones and distributed defense manufacturing.

sections.heading: World Court Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide; Mexico Captures 'El Chapo Isidro'
sections.body:
New York Times, CNA, BBC, and AP News — Major legal and security milestones closed the week across Asia, the Americas, and global climate diplomacy. In The Hague, the International Court of Justice ruled Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in 2017, a landmark precedent welcomed by Ankara and UN leadership (New York Times, Anadolu Agency), while Vietnam's National Assembly abolished the death penalty for drug trafficking (CNA).

In the Americas, Mexican troops captured FBI top-ten fugitive drug lord Fausto Isidro Meza Flores ('El Chapo Isidro') in a firefight that killed 11, a federal judge approved a $7 billion Roundup cancer settlement, and a 6.8-magnitude quake shook Peru (TRT World, BBC, New York Times, Reuters). Meanwhile in Antalya, UN COP31 climate talks spilled into a second day of overtime as 196 nations clashed over fossil fuel transition language and climate finance (AP News, DW).
sections.whyItMatters: The World Court's genocide ruling sets a binding state-accountability benchmark, while COP31's overtime deadlock underscores widening North-South rifts over decarbonization financing.

bottomLine: The week of November 16–22 exposed deep fractures beneath headline summits and mega-IPOs: Trump, Xi, and Putin's Shenzhen meeting left Europe and Ukraine on the sidelines just as Russian missiles struck Poland, Anthropic's $1.5 trillion debut gave way to an SEC probe of Nvidia and a $4 trillion AI rout, and Iranian strikes on Bahrain showed Gulf escalation continuing despite softer oil prices.
